extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, and students of literary theory/poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama — how to construct plot, characters, and dramatic parts so the piece produces the proper tragic effects (pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as a whole (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is complete and whole; a whole is that which has a beginning, middle, and end. A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end is that which itself naturally follows some other thing and has nothing following it; a middle both follows and is followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to this type. The parts must be organically connected so that removal or displacement of a part disjoints the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude / length
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of a certain magnitude: not exceedingly small (confused or imperceptible) nor excessively large (cannot be taken in at once); length should be such as may be easily embraced by the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude is tied to the nature of the drama: within limits, greater length may be more beautiful provided the whole is perspicuous. Proper magnitude admits a change from bad fortune to good or vice versa according to probability or necessity. Practical limits (e.g., competitive performance hours) are not part of artistic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in imitating one action which is a whole; unity of the hero is not required (a single man's life has many incidents and cannot be reduced to one action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must centre on one action so that all parts are necessary to the unity; incidents without contribution to the whole are not organic parts. Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey show centering on one action despite many events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity (what may happen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should represent what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity (not merely what has happened). Poetry expresses the universal (what a person of given character would do), unlike history which records particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events should be credible under probability/necessity; the poet may invent names or adapt legends so long as the action is possible and probable. Plots should derive events from preceding actions by necessity or probability, not by chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker of plots (priority of action over versification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker (poet) should be maker of plots rather than of verses, since the poet imitates actions; if an historical subject is used, the author is still a poet provided the events have internal probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize plot construction and causal coherence; versification alone does not make a poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (epeisodic) construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots — where episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence — are the worst type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic writing often stems from extending plot for competitive/performative reasons; it breaks natural continuity and should be avoided. Good poets avoid plots that are merely a string of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and causal sequence (tragic wonder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that come by surprise and at the same time follow one another (are causally linked) produce the strongest tragic wonder; wonders arising from apparent design are more striking than mere accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct surprises that are nevertheless the necessary or probable result of earlier actions, not pure chance; examples include statues or incidents that seem designed rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs. complicated plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple when the turning point is reached without Reversal or Recognition; Complicated when reached with Reversal of Fortune or Recognition or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types are possible; where complications occur (reversal/recognition), they must arise from the plot's internal structure and follow by necessity or probability. (Note: the text treats the relative merits of simple and complex designs in different passages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of fortune (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reversal of Fortune is a change by which a train of action produces the opposite of the effect intended, according to the rule of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should result from antecedent actions and be credible within the plot (example: the messenger in Oedipus attempting consolation but producing ruin). They are powerful when they are necessary or probable consequences rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; best when coincident with Reversal of Fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition should be closely related to the plot/action (often recognition of persons); combined with reversal it produces pity and fear. Recognitions may be of persons or of facts (who did or did not do something).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic incident / pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident (pathos) is a destructive or painful action such as death on stage, bodily torments, wounds, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidents contribute to the tragic effect but are most effective when they arise naturally from the plot’s structure (not gratuitous spectacle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best structural device: reversal + recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form is when Recognition and Reversal coincide (as in Oedipus), producing the strongest tragic effect of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, aim for recognitions that coincide with reversals arising necessarily from the plot; other forms (recognition without reversal, reversal without recognition) are less powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) requirements — four qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Four aspects of character to be considered: (1) that it be good (chrestos), (2) that it be appropriate/fitting to the person (harmonizing with sex, rank, role), (3) that it be like (similar/probable), (4) that it be consistent/regular (homalos — not anomalous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be plausibly good enough to inspire pity when they fall, not eminently virtuous nor utterly villainous. Do not confer unseemly traits on a character (e.g., undue bravery on a woman) or create inconsistent/unnatural behaviour. Seek the likely or necessary action for the character (either by necessity or probability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral profile for tragic protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should not be eminently good and just, nor an utter villain; rather someone of some repute and prosperity whose downfall is brought about by some error or frailty (hamartia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots of a perfectly good man brought to misfortune (shocking but not tragic) or the downfall of a thoroughly bad man (satisfies moral sense but arouses neither pity nor fear). The ideal is a figure like Oedipus or Thyestes — notable, neither perfectly virtuous nor depraved, undone by error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single action preference (single rather than double plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single rather than double (one unified action rather than two interwoven threads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-threaded plots (like the Odyssey) may please audiences but yield a different (weaker or non-true-tragic) pleasure. Single unified action better achieves tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of agents for pity/fear (who the act occurs between)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that arouse pity and fear should occur between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; strongest effect arises when the incident occurs between those near or dear to one another (kinship or friendship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts between enemies or indifferent persons arouse less pity/fear; seek situations like brother against brother, son against father, mother against child, etc. Traditional legends may be used but should be handled with invention and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plot-internal origination of terror over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacle (scenic presentment) but better and more artistic when produced by the inner structure of the piece so that even a listener (without sight) would be moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely first on plot construction to produce tragic effects; excessive dependence on spectacle, monstrous effects, or stage contrivances is less artistic and often indicates weakness in the poet's craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic quantitative parts (structural elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts that function as elements of the whole: Prologos (part before parodos), Parodos (first choral utterance), Stasimon (choral ode without anapaests/trochees), Episodes (sections between choral songs), Exodos (part after which there is no choral song), Commos (joint lament of chorus and actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know and employ these parts appropriately; they are distinct functional units within the tragic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitions must follow from composition (necessity or probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions (changes, shifts) in the plot must occur from the composition of the myth so that from antecedent events the subsequent ones happen either by necessity or according to probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between events that happen 'because of this' and those 'after this' — ensure the former for coherent tragedy; avoid arbitrary or purely convenienced transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and suitability in incidents (seek the necessary or probable)
rubrics_metrics.description: In both the constitution of events and in characters one should always seek either the necessary or the probable so that the things done or said be necessary or credible for the situation and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid actions or speeches that are unseemly, anomalous, or inappropriate to the character’s sex, class, or role; prefer the likely or necessary course of action.
